entities.name: Guard backhands Benjamin Jonson, knocking him and the chair to the ground

entities.name: Benjamin Jonson's nose begins to bleed after being struck

entities.name: Guards strike Benjamin Jonson again, causing him to spit out a tooth

entities.name: Interrogator clarifies interest in plays received from Edward de Vere

document_metadata.title: 14、EXT. ROSE THEATER/BANKSIDE LONDON - CONTINUOUS
document_metadata.summary: Southampton and Oxford approach the Rose Theater; Southampton excited, Oxford skeptical. After teasing about elitism, they enter, leaving retainers behind, as Oxford jokingly worries about puppets.

entities.name: Nashe drinks ale and comments on Jonson's play
entities.description: Nashe takes a swig of ale and remarks that Jonson's second play is nearly drawing a full audience, expressing admiration for his wit.

entities.name: Marlowe criticizes Jonson's wit as buried and worthless
entities.description: Marlowe responds to Nashe by comparing Jonson's wit to a grain of wheat hidden in chaff, claiming it is difficult to find and not valuable when discovered.

entities.name: Dekker requests money from Marlowe for unpaid work
entities.description: Dekker asks Marlowe to lend him a few pence, explaining that Henslowe still owes him payment for his play "Shoemaker's Holiday".

entities.name: Marlowe dismisses the value of Dekker's play
entities.description: Marlowe hands over coins but retorts that Henslowe hasn't paid Dekker because no one saw "Shoemaker's Holiday", implying its lack of success.

entities.name: Marlowe is alerted to Southampton's presence in the theater
entities.description: Nashe points out to Marlowe that Southampton, one of his unrequited loves, is seated in the box, prompting Marlowe to look across the theater.

entities.name: Marlowe expresses dismay at Southampton's company
entities.description: Upon seeing Southampton with the Earl of Oxford, Marlowe frowns and voices disappointment that Southampton would prefer the company of older, less appealing men.

entities.name: Nashe identifies the Earl of Oxford in the theater box
entities.description: Nashe confirms that the man with Southampton is the Earl of Oxford, recalling that he once employed his own acting troupe for court performances.

entities.name: Dekker considers submitting material to the Earl of Oxford
entities.description: Dekker wonders aloud whether the Earl of Oxford might be in need of new plays or writings to support his theatrical interests.

entities.name: Marlowe rejects Dekker's work as unsuitable for Oxford
entities.description: Marlowe scoffs at the idea that the Earl of Oxford would be interested in any of Dekker's material, dismissing it as unworthy.

entities.name: Nashe reveals Oxford's estrangement from the Queen and current reclusiveness
entities.description: Nashe explains that Oxford had a falling out with the Queen years ago and is now more of a recluse than an active patron of the arts.

entities.name: Shakespeare mocks Fastidious on stage with exaggerated insults
entities.description: On stage, Shakespeare points to the character Fastidious and launches into a comedic rant, calling him a fool and mocking his appearance and habits.

entities.name: Shakespeare performs a satirical portrayal of Fastidious's nightly and daily rituals
entities.description: Shakespeare claims Fastidious sleeps with a musk-cat and walks hung with perfumed chains as penance, drawing loud laughter from the groundlings.

entities.name: Groundling identifies with the joke about unpleasant smell
entities.description: A groundling shouts out in response to Shakespeare's joke, jokingly claiming to have been the source of the bad smell, which amuses the lower audience further.

entities.name: Shakespeare elaborates on Fastidious's absurd attempts at personal grooming
entities.description: Shakespeare continues his satire by claiming Fastidious tans his skin in civet to preserve his youth and please his lady, while also mocking his lack of intelligence.

entities.name: Nobleman storms out of the theater in anger at the satire
entities.description: A nobleman wearing a feathered hat stands up in fury during Shakespeare's performance, interpreting the satire as a personal attack, and exits with his lady.

entities.name: Audience laughs at the offended nobleman's departure
entities.description: As the nobleman leaves in anger, the audience erupts in laughter, mocking his reaction and reinforcing the comedic triumph of the performance.

entities.name: Shakespeare revels in the audience's reaction to his performance
entities.description: Shakespeare smiles triumphantly on stage, clearly pleased by the audience's roaring laughter and the visible impact of his satire.

document_metadata.title: 16、INT. A JAIL CELL - DAY
document_metadata.summary: Jonson is thrown into a crowded cell after being insulted; Essex voices concerns about societal unrest, taxation, Spanish dominance, and Catholic plots.

entities.description: Jonson is forcefully thrown into a prison cell by unseen guards or captors, indicating a sudden incarceration.

entities.name: Prison cell door is slammed shut
entities.description: The door of the prison cell is forcefully closed behind Jonson, emphasizing the abruptness and finality of his confinement.

entities.name: Jonson curses the guard and his lineage
entities.description: After being locked in the cell, Jonson shouts a verbal insult at the door, cursing both the guard and the guard's father as an expression of anger and defiance.

entities.name: Jonson surveys the other prisoners in the cell
entities.description: Jonson looks around the cell and observes that it is already occupied by a dozen or so other imprisoned individuals.

entities.name: Essex delivers a monologue on political unrest
entities.description: From off-screen, Essex speaks about widespread social and political turmoil, including oppressive taxation, Spanish dominance in the New World, Irish rebellion, and pervasive Catholic conspiracies.

document_metadata.title: 24、INT. HEDINGHAM CASTLE - KITCHEN - LATER
document_metadata.summary: Boy Oxford impresses Young Elizabeth with his poetry and declares his desire to serve her in war and state, charming her while amusingly provoking William Cecil's disapproval of his play.

entities.name: Boy Oxford removes costume and make-up backstage
entities.description: Boy Oxford, still partially in character with his winged costume, sits before a makeshift mirror and begins taking off his theatrical attire and makeup along with other young actors after a performance.

entities.name: Young Elizabeth and her court enter the backstage area
entities.description: Young Elizabeth, accompanied by members of her senior court including William Cecil and John De Vere, enters the makeshift backstage area, causing an immediate hush among the young actors.

entities.name: Boy Oxford bows before Young Elizabeth
entities.description: Upon noticing Young Elizabeth's arrival, Boy Oxford performs a deep bow in her presence as a sign of respect and deference to her royal status.

entities.name: Young Elizabeth questions Boy Oxford about authorship of the play
entities.description: Young Elizabeth addresses Boy Oxford directly, expressing interest in whether he truly authored the evening's performance, prompting him to seek permission from his father before responding.

entities.name: Boy Oxford confirms he wrote the play
entities.description: With his father's nod of approval, Boy Oxford replies to Young Elizabeth that he indeed composed the play performed that evening.

entities.name: Young Elizabeth commands Boy Oxford to compose an impromptu poem on truth
entities.description: Young Elizabeth challenges Boy Oxford to create a spontaneous poem, specifying 'Truth' as the subject, testing his wit and poetic skill in real time.

entities.name: Boy Oxford recites an impromptu poem about truth
entities.description: Boy Oxford composes and delivers a short verse asserting the enduring nature of truth, stating that time cannot falsify what was once true, impressing his audience.

entities.name: Young Elizabeth reacts with approval to the poem
entities.description: After hearing Boy Oxford's verse, Young Elizabeth smiles and claps in appreciation, acknowledging his poetic talent and composure under pressure.

document_metadata.title: 61、INT. THE MERMAID'S TAVERN - DAY
document_metadata.summary: Shakespeare announces 'Romeo' will run for a fortnight; others react skeptically, with Nashe doubting his ability to replicate success, while Marlowe dismisses romantic tragedies.

entities.name: Group of playwrights reacts to performance of Romeo and Juliet
entities.description: Jonson, Marlowe, Dekker, and Nashe sit together in silence after attending a performance of 'Romeo and Juliet', visibly shocked and processing what they witnessed.

entities.name: Nashe claims he could write in iambic pentameter
entities.description: Nashe, slightly intoxicated, asserts that writing in iambic pentameter is not difficult and claims he could do it if he wanted to.

entities.name: Marlowe questions Nashe's assertion about verse writing
entities.description: Marlowe challenges Nashe by asking him to clarify his statement about the ease of writing in iambic pentameter.

entities.name: Dekker points out that the play was not entirely in verse
entities.description: Dekker observes that 'Romeo and Juliet' included non-verse sections, which Nashe then uses to argue that writing such a play is even easier.

entities.name: Post-Performance Gathering Of Playwrights And Actors
entities.description: A social gathering following the performance of 'Romeo and Juliet', attended by playwrights and actors, where they discuss the play and its form.
entities.summary: A social gathering following the performance of 'Romeo and Juliet', attended by playwrights and actors, where they discuss the play and its form.

entities.name: Twenty-seven years later
entities.description: A relative temporal expression indicating the scene occurs two decades after a prior event, anchoring the current gathering in time.

entities.description: A specific setting within the scene where the group of playwrights is seated, serving as the immediate physical location of the dialogue.

entities.name: Ben Jonson
entities.description: A playwright present at the post-performance gathering, reacting to the performance of Romeo and Juliet and engaging in conversation about verse writing.
entities.summary: A man rushes to a theater with a manuscript, while another hides underneath as soldiers led by Pole search. A bound man is pushed in, witnesses chaos, and is taken by longboat to the Tower of London; a young man watches silently from backstage.

entities.name: Marlowe
entities.description: A playwright who questions Nashe's claim about writing in iambic pentameter after the performance of Romeo and Juliet.
entities.summary: A playwright critiques Jonson and Dekker, reacts to Southampton, challenges peers, admires Henry V, questions Nashe on iambic pentameter, and discusses metaphorical murder with Pole regarding a production shutdown.

entities.name: Dekker
entities.description: A playwright who observes that the play was not entirely in verse during the post-performance discussion.
entities.summary: A playwright interacts with Marlowe, Nashe, and others in theater and tavern settings, observes a play's verse structure, questions Essex's sponsorship, and reacts to a coat-of-arms, reflecting literary and social dynamics among contemporary writers.

entities.name: Nashe
entities.description: A playwright who, slightly drunk, claims he could write in iambic pentameter after watching Romeo and Juliet.
entities.summary: A group of playwrights and associates, including Marlowe's companion and a friend of Shakespeare, react to a theater performance, authorship, and coat-of-arms, with drunken remarks, confusion, and applause for an anonymous writer.

entities.name: mugs of ale
entities.description: Drinking vessels containing ale that the playwrights hold during the post-performance gathering.

entities.name: Shakespeare announces Henslowe's decision to run Romeo for a fortnight
entities.description: Shakespeare excitedly informs the group that Henslowe wants the play 'Romeo' to continue running for two weeks, treating it as remarkable news.

entities.name: Shakespeare calls for a round of drinks to celebrate
entities.description: Shakespeare attempts to order drinks for everyone at the gathering by calling out to the innkeeper, first formally and then by the name Billy when there is no response.

entities.name: Shakespeare goes to the bar to fetch drinks
entities.description: After receiving no response from calling out, Shakespeare personally moves to the bar to obtain the drinks.

entities.name: Nashe expresses doubt about Shakespeare's future success
entities.description: Nashe reacts to the news of the play's extension by dismissing Shakespeare as a 'one-trick pony' who won't be able to replicate his success.

entities.name: Dekker comments on the popularity of romantic tragedies with maids
entities.description: Dekker observes that the play's success is due in part to the maids' fondness for romantic tragedies.

entities.name: Marlowe expresses disdain for romantic tragedies
entities.description: Marlowe states his deliberate avoidance of romantic tragedies, implying a lack of artistic value in the genre.

entities.name: bar

entities.name: William Shakespeare
entities.description: A playwright who excitedly announces that Henslowe has decided to run 'Romeo' for a fortnight and calls for a round of drinks to celebrate.
entities.summary: A renowned playwright, possibly Shakespeare, known for 'Romeo and Juliet,' is depicted as skeptical of poetry's idealistic power, engaging with Jonson on manuscripts, performing satirically, and interacting on London Bridge, with his identity questioned due to scarce personal records.

document_metadata.summary: Oxford, wounded by Beaulieu during a fencing duel, kills him in self-defense. Francesco arrives to find Oxford injured and Beaulieu dead, learning it was an assassination attempt.

document_metadata.summary: Shakespeare confronts Jonson over betrayal and demands payment, suspecting Jonson killed Kit; he later disguises himself to avoid detection while tensions escalate at the bear-baiting pit.

document_metadata.summary: Elizabeth spares Southampton due to Cecil's loyalty, not Oxford's plea; Oxford secures his son's future posthumously, ensuring unity under James, while Elizabeth condemns his legacy.

entities.name: Oxford approaches Elizabeth in the throne room
entities.description: Oxford enters the throne room as Elizabeth sits surrounded by courtiers, and he walks toward her while ignoring the others present.

entities.name: Oxford bows before Elizabeth
entities.description: Upon reaching Elizabeth, Oxford performs a deep bow in her presence as a sign of respect or submission.

entities.name: Elizabeth orders courtiers to leave the chamber
entities.description: Elizabeth commands everyone in the room to depart so she can speak privately with Oxford.

entities.name: Robert Cecil resists Elizabeth's order to leave
entities.description: Robert Cecil hesitates and attempts to stay in the chamber despite Elizabeth's command for all to leave.

entities.name: Cecil exits after being ordered again by Elizabeth
entities.description: After Elizabeth reiterates her command, Cecil leaves the room, visibly concerned about the private encounter.

entities.name: Elizabeth accuses Oxford of causing rebellion
entities.description: Elizabeth confronts Oxford, blaming him for inciting public unrest through his play and words, and accuses him of plotting against her.

entities.name: Oxford confesses fatherhood and pleads for Southampton
entities.description: Oxford reveals that he and Elizabeth have a son together—Southampton—and offers his own life in place of his son's execution.

entities.name: Oxford kneels before Elizabeth in submission
entities.description: In a gesture of surrender and desperation, Oxford drops to his knees before Elizabeth during their emotional confrontation.

entities.name: Elizabeth turns away from Oxford in anger
entities.description: Overcome with emotion, Elizabeth walks to the window and turns her back on Oxford, refusing to face him.

entities.name: Oxford denies conspiracy against Elizabeth
entities.description: Oxford insists that neither he nor the others ever plotted against Elizabeth, stating their true target was Robert Cecil for corrupting the monarchy.

entities.name: Private Audience Between Oxford And Elizabeth
entities.description: A secluded and emotionally charged meeting between Oxford and Queen Elizabeth, held in the throne room after all courtiers are dismissed.

entities.summary: A nobleman observes events at the Globe and a tennis match, listens silently to Southampton and Essex, warns of political dangers from the Cecils, and reflects on the Tudor rose while acknowledging his role in freeing Ben Jonson.

entities.name: Queen Elizabeth
entities.description: The aging queen, visibly ill, who confronts Oxford in a private audience, accusing him of inciting rebellion through his writings and refusing to spare Southampton initially.
entities.summary: Queen Elizabeth attends court performances, reacts with delight and discomfort during plays, receives counsel from William Cecil, mourns his death by placing his cane in his coffin, and is attended by ladies-in-waiting.

entities.name: Robert Cecil
entities.description: A courtier and advisor who resists Elizabeth's order to leave the chamber, showing concern before exiting under direct command.
entities.summary: William Cecil's family, including his sons and a hunchbacked boy, are involved in court intrigues surrounding a controversial play; one son receives it as a gift, another eavesdrops on the queen, while Cecil confronts a man about Essex and opposes the play's performance.

entities.name: William Shakespeare
entities.description: A playwright referenced in the context of a plot with Oxford, whose works are implied to have been used as tools of political influence or rebellion.
entities.summary: A renowned playwright, possibly Shakespeare, known for 'Romeo and Juliet,' is depicted as skeptical of poetry's idealistic power, engaging with Jonson on manuscripts, performing satirically, and interacting on London Bridge, with his identity questioned due to scarce personal records.

entities.name: Southampton
entities.description: The son of Oxford and Elizabeth, accused of high treason and facing execution, whose fate is the central point of negotiation in the private audience.
entities.summary: A nobleman associated with Marlowe and the Earl of Oxford attends a play at the Globe, engages in political discussions with Essex about royal succession, and is seen before a tennis match as an opponent to Essex.

entities.name: courtiers
entities.description: A group of royal attendants present in the throne room who serve as witnesses to the initial encounter between Oxford and Elizabeth before being dismissed.

entities.name: Elizabeth praises the Cecils for protecting her throne
entities.description: Elizabeth declares that despite numerous threats from foreign and domestic powers, only the Cecils remained trustworthy and loyal, ensuring her survival and reign.

entities.name: Elizabeth rejects Oxford's claim of loyalty
entities.description: Elizabeth mocks Oxford's assertion that he and the Earls would have protected her, emphasizing that they were among those who conspired against her.

entities.name: Oxford pleads for Southampton's life
entities.description: Oxford appeals to Elizabeth to let their child, Southampton, live, showing paternal concern and desperation.

entities.name: Elizabeth suffers a coughing fit
entities.description: Elizabeth is overcome by a sudden coughing fit, momentarily interrupting the conversation with Oxford.

entities.name: Oxford waits patiently for Elizabeth to recover
entities.description: Oxford remains silent and composed, waiting for Elizabeth to regain her composure after her coughing fit.

entities.name: Elizabeth questions if Southampton knows the truth
entities.description: Elizabeth asks Oxford whether Southampton is aware of his true parentage, seeking confirmation of his ignorance.

entities.name: Oxford confirms Southampton does not know the truth
entities.description: Oxford silently indicates that Southampton is unaware of his parentage, reinforcing his commitment to secrecy.

entities.name: Elizabeth agrees to let Oxford take Southampton
entities.description: After a moment of contemplation, Elizabeth consents to allow Oxford to take Southampton, under the condition of absolute secrecy.

entities.name: Oxford expresses relief with a smile
entities.description: Upon hearing Elizabeth's decision, Oxford allows himself a small, relieved smile, showing emotional release.

entities.name: Oxford sets conditions for claiming Southampton
entities.description: Oxford insists that he will only claim Southampton after his own death, following James's secure ascension to the throne, to ensure national unity.

entities.name: Oxford declares his final gift to England
entities.description: Oxford proclaims that ensuring a unified kingdom under one king, despite James being a Scot, will be his ultimate contribution to the nation.

entities.name: Oxford vows to remain publicly untainted
entities.description: Oxford asserts that he will maintain the image of purity and detachment, never publicly acknowledging his son or his role in the royal lineage.

entities.name: Elizabeth condemns Oxford's legacy as treasonous
entities.description: Elizabeth declares that Oxford's relationship with her, his son, and his plays will never be acknowledged or claimed by her or the crown.

entities.description: Elizabeth leaves the throne room, ending the private audience and walking away from Oxford without further acknowledgment.

entities.description: Oxford remains in the throne room, silently observing Elizabeth as she departs, reflecting on the outcome of their encounter.
